A police officer has told an inquest that the day she tried to disarm a mother who was harming herself inside a Darwin domestic violence shelter was "one of the worst days" of her career.

The coroner is examining the death of 33-year-old mother Toko-Harieta Maki inside the shelter on the morning of July 25, 2024.

The inquest will continue on Thursday, when it will be evidence from senior police and NT Department of Children and Families staff.

Warning: This article contains references to self-harm and content some readers may find distressing.

An inquest has heard evidence from a senior police officer who ran into a room to disarm a mother who was self-harming inside a Darwin crisis accommodation facility, describing the incident as "one of the worst days" of her policing career.

The inquest, presided over by Northern Territory Coroner Elisabeth Armitage, has this week been probing the events surrounding the death of Toko-Harieta Maki, who died on the morning of July 25, 2024.

The 33-year-old mother from New Zealand had fled a violent relationship five days earlier, and alleged her partner had refused to let her take their seven-month-old baby.

On Wednesday, the court heard that at around 8:12am on the day of the incident, two NT Police officers arrived at the domestic violence refuge where she was sheltering, to assist St John Ambulance paramedics by disarming Ms Maki.

Elisabeth Armitage is presiding over the inquest. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin )

In confronting body-worn video that was played to the court, the mother could be heard screaming inside a locked room while paramedics briefed police officers outside.

The court previously heard paramedics arrived at the facility at 7:58am and spent just 23 seconds inside the room — where Ms Maki could be seen harming herself with a knife, surrounded by blood — before they stepped back out to await police assistance, letting the door lock behind them.

The footage then showed police and paramedics growing frustrated as they searched for a shelter staff member with a key to the room, and at one point discussed breaking in through a window.

"It was one of the worst days in my policing career," the officer told the court.

The court heard roughly six minutes after police arrived — almost an hour after Ms Maki had first called Triple Zero (000) — they gained access to her room.

NT Police had been called to assist paramedics at the scene. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish )

"When that door opened, I was not fully prepared for what I saw," the officer told the court.

"[The paramedic] did not convey to me that she is significantly bleeding inside and we need to get in there ASAP."

She told the court she found Ms Maki sitting on the floor "actively self-harming" and that the woman was "fighting" with police as they tried to remove the knife she was using.

"She kicked the doorframe … she just kept screaming 'Jesus cut it off'," the officer said.

The inquest heard police placed Ms Maki in handcuffs to stop her from self-harming.

The death is being examined as a death in custody.

When asked what support NT Police had offered her in the aftermath, the officer said she had received a single email outlining various support services she could reach out to, but she had not had time to process the incident when it arrived.

"I heard nothing until we were summoned to this inquest," she said.

Judge Armitage said NT Police had a duty of care to ensure its frontline responders were offered professional support, and requested the force provide a statement outlining what services had been offered by the end of the coronial.

"Police understand that exposure to traumatic incidents, harms."

Under cross-examination by NT Police lawyer Fiona Kepert, the officer conceded she had also received regular check-ins from her police sergeant.

The coroner said NT Police had a duty to provide staff with professional support where necessary. ( ABC News: Hamish Harty )

Over the past three days, the inquest has heard Ms Maki had been desperately trying to regain custody of her son before her death.

It also heard Ms Maki, along with other agencies, had made several complaints about domestic violence against the partner.

Despite this, both the NT Police and the NT Department of Children and Families separately found there was no risk to the baby staying with his father.

In a distressing video recorded on a smartphone before she fled, which was played to the court on Wednesday, Ms Maki and her partner could be heard arguing, with their baby in the background.

At one point in the video, Ms Maki expressed pain before her partner repeatedly yelled, "come here".

Later, he could be heard threatening her: "I'm going to flog you black and blue".

The inquest heard distressing accounts of domestic violence. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish )

Earlier in the inquest, a family violence specialist who had been Ms Maki's case manager at the refuge testified that the mother had alleged her partner was abusive and that their baby had been exposed to the violence.

The specialist also described a large tattoo on Ms Maki's body, which stated she was her partner's "property".

"She was terrified for her safety, but more so for her child's safety," the case manager told the court.

"The night before she ran, he had the baby as he was punching her and — when she made him aware — he threw the baby in the cot.

"I told all this to child protections."

The inquest into Ms Maki's death is due to continue tomorrow, when the court is expected to hear evidence from senior police and NT Department of Children and Families staff.

Rodrigo Duterte was not present for the court hearing, with his defence saying he was not mentally fit. ( AP: Bullit Marquez )

ICC judges have thrown out a court challenge against former Philippines president Rodrigo Duterte's crimes against humanity charges.

February hearings heard Mr Duterte was allegedly responsible for thousands of deaths during his war on drugs.

If the trial proceeds it would be the first against a former head of state from Asia.

Former Philippines president Rodrigo Duterte could still stand trial over his war on drugs after International Criminal Court (ICC) judges threw out a court challenge.

The 81-year-old faces three counts of crimes against humanity at the international court based in The Hague over murders allegedly committed as part of his crackdown on drug users and pushers.

The allegations relate to his time as mayor of Davao city between 2013 and 2016, and then as president until March 2019 when the Philippines withdrew from the ICC.

Mr Duterte's defence had argued the court had no jurisdiction over alleged crimes in the Philippines because the country is no longer subject to the Rome Statute, the ICC's founding text.

Maria Espinosa, the mother of a drug war victim, during the initial hearings for Rodrigo Duterte. ( Reuters: Noel Celis )

The prosecution countered the alleged crimes occurred while the Philippines was still a member of the ICC and so judges can rule on Mr Duterte's case.

In an initial decision in October, the ICC pre-trial chamber sided with the prosecution, ruling the investigation into Mr Duterte began before the Philippines withdrawal.

The appeals court threw out the defence team's challenge of that decision.

The court "has rejected all four grounds of appeal," said presiding judge Luz del Carmen Ibáñez Carranza.

Mr Duterte's defence lawyer Nicholas Kaufman said he was not surprised by the verdict given the fact that Mr Duterte's trial is the one remaining high-profile case at the ICC.

"Allowing the appeal would have practically emptied the Court's docket," he said in a statement to AFP.

Former Philippines president Rodrigo Duterte personally drew up "death lists" and boasted about murders committed during his "war on drugs", an International Criminal Court prosecutor alleges at a crimes against humanity hearing.

In a separate procedure, judges are weighing whether to confirm the charges against Mr Duterte, the final step before a trial, which would be the first against a former head of state from Asia.

At hearings in February the prosecution alleged Mr Duterte was responsible for thousands of deaths during his war on drugs.

His defence said there was no "smoking gun" directly linking Mr Duterte's fiery rhetoric and threats against drug users and actual murders.

In any case, Mr Duterte is unlikely to appear in court.

A protester rallies against Rodrigo Duterte. ( Reuters: Noel Celis )

The court granted his request not to appear for the hearings in February, with his defence saying he was not mentally fit.

The only time he has been seen since his arrest and transfer to The Hague was at an initial appearance via videolink at which he came across as confused and exhausted.

He did not appear at Thursday's reading of the decision.

Topic: Federal - State Issues

Mark Butler expects his state and territory counterparts to get on board with his sweeping overhaul of the NDIS. ( ABC News )

Labor's plan to rein in NDIS growth will result in more than 160,000 people shifting off the scheme, with states expected to deliver alternative "foundational supports".

Experts and states warn systems may not be ready for the demand surge, but Health Minister Mark Butler is confident they will cope.

The federal government will release legislation and negotiate with the Coalition to pass reforms, while states plan to consult with the disability community about changes.

Labor expects states and territories to step up and deliver more disability supports as thousands of Australians are shifted off the NDIS, amid concerns they will struggle to meet demand.

Federal Health Minister Mark Butler has said he was confident his state and territory counterparts would get on board, despite resistance from the Queensland government and calls for more detail from other jurisdictions.

State and territory disability ministers were briefed by Mr Butler and federal NDIS Minister Jenny McAlister late on Wednesday after the sweeping reforms were announced .

Mr Butler acknowledged that states wanted to see "more detail" and confirmed he would share the legislation behind the changes with them.

"We're providing [states] huge amounts of additional money to run their hospitals, and in return they committed — in writing — to support this disability reform direction and to implement the Thriving Kids deal," he told 730.

Health Minister Mark Butler has unveiled the government's plan to curb the ballooning growth of the NDIS and save the budget a projected $35 billion over four years.

The Albanese government's changes aim to halve the current annual growth rate of the NDIS, reducing the total spending to about $55 billion instead of a forecast $70 billion by 2030.

To achieve this, Labor will look to remove more than 160,000 participants from the scheme by the end of the decade by narrowing eligibility to people with significant functional impairment and shifting some supports outside the NDIS via state-run "foundational supports".

It will also rein in unscheduled plan reassessments and reset social and community participation spending to 2023 levels, while creating a $200 million Inclusive Communities Fund.

Mark Butler reveals the changes during a speech to the National Press Club. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts )

Labor will need the Coalition's support to get the NDIS changes through the federal parliament after the Greens signalled they would oppose reforms.

The plan also heavily relies on states and territories delivering on a broad agreement to provide support to participants no longer eligible for the scheme.

In 2023, states, territories and the Commonwealth agreed to provision $10 billion for so-called foundational supports to assist Australians with low to moderate needs as an alternative to the NDIS.

With more changes surrounding the NDIS set to be announced, here’s everything you need to know about the scheme.

About $4 billion was earmarked for the establishment of what has become known as the Thriving Kids program, which is due to start rolling out in October and be fully established by 2027.

The remaining $6 billion remains available to reinstate and develop state-based supports for both young people and adults who have low or moderate needs.

How these funds will be spent will depend on NDIS eligibility changes due to be finalised by the end of this year, but examples could include state-based transport assistance or group therapy sessions run through existing community organisations.

All jurisdictions bar Queensland have signed bilateral agreements with the Commonwealth to operate the Thriving Kids program.

Queensland Disability Services Minister Amanda Camm accused the Albanese government of failing to properly regulate the NDIS.

"[They] have allowed dodgy, shonky individuals and companies to take advantage of those with a disability right across the state," she said.

David Cullen, former chief economist at the National Disability Insurance Agency, agreed there were too many people on the NDIS and described the reforms as "brutal, but necessary".

But he raised concerns about the capacity of state and territory governments to meet the increased demand for services from those moved off the scheme.

Health Minister Mark Butler has unveiled sweeping cuts to the ballooning National Disability Insurance Scheme, aimed at cutting costs of the program down to $55 billion by the end of the decade.

"There are a lot of people on the scheme who should never have been on the scheme, but the trouble is that all the services that they used to support them are gone now," Mr Cullen said.

"The states don't seem to show very much interest in putting those back together again, so we've got to go slowly."

Speaking at the National Press Club on Wednesday, Mr Butler said previous supports that had operated "really well" before the NDIS include programs that offered people with psychosocial disabilities "personal helpers and mentors" and "day-to-day living" services.

"The problem has been that, as the NDIS has taken in so much of the government funding in this space, those services have been either wound back or, in some cases, dismantled," he said.

"And all state and territory and Commonwealth governments have a responsibility to rebuild them."

Tasmanian Disability Services Minister Jo Palmer said she understood the federal government's announcement might be a source of "uncertainty" for her state's community.

Western Australian Disability Services Minister Hannah Beazley said the state government "will be making it clear to the Commonwealth that it should not push the cost burden onto the states".

A New South Wales government spokesman said they would "carefully review the announcements and the impact they have on NSW".

And a Victorian government spokesperson said they would "continue to advocate to the Commonwealth so that no one misses out on the services they need".

Shadow NDIS Minister Melissa McIntosh accused Labor of dropping a "bomb" on the disability community by announcing "savage cuts and functional assessments" for all participants on the scheme.

"Rather than targeting the fraud and rorting that has infiltrated the scheme, the Albanese Labor government has decided to target people with disability to find their budget saves," she said.

She said the opposition supported "sensible reforms" to stop the "fraud, rorts and waste" in the NDIS and would work with the government to tackle those issues.

Melissa McIntosh accuses Labor of dropping a "bomb" on the disability community. ( ABC News: Callum Flinn )

While the Coalition is awaiting the details from Labor on the specific legislation, multiple Liberal sources told the ABC there was broad support in the party room for reining in NDIS costs.

Greens disability spokesman Senator Jordon Steele-John described the NDIS proposal as a "betrayal" by Labor.

"Disabled people are now left dreading whether they will be one of the 160,000 people Labor plans to kick off the NDIS — because their disability is too invisible, or because a computer predicts they will be fine without supports," he said.

Former NDIS minister Bill Shorten told the ABC he was "pleased" the government was continuing his crackdown on fraud in the scheme.

Mr Shorten said the reforms announced by Mr Butler followed the blueprint of a 2023 review that recommended reforms like increasing registration of providers.

"They're continuing to do broadly what was planned with some differences based on changing facts, like the unexpected [cost] blowout," he said.
